about: Proofs of open problems accepted by Lean are merged and credited at once. They count as an open problem solved only once the formal statement has been checked against the original problem (confirmed). flagged: the formal statement does not say what the problem says, so the open problem is not solved. known: listed as open upstream, but already settled in the literature (the Lean proof is a formalization of a known result).

Erdos1066.erdos_1066.variants.higher_dim.note: This is a genuine disproof by construction. It uses a Kerdock-set (Kantor-Williams) two-angle configuration in dimension d=3q (q=2^(2t+1)) with n=2q^2 points. All squared norms are b and all inner products are +-a, with b=1/2+a, so the minimum distance is 1. A Gram-sum argument shows that any subset with all pairwise distances >1 has at most k+2 ~ sqrt(2q)+2 points, whereas c*n/d = 2cq/3; this refutes any uniform constant c. gDim faithfully encodes Erdős's g_d(n). The 'constant independent of d and n' reading is the only meaningful one: erdosproblems.com itself calls the upper bound g_d(n) << n/d 'trivial' via widely spaced simplices, and for fixed d the bound holds with a d-dependent constant (kissing number). erdosproblems.com/1066 is open, with 0 proof claims and no forum comment on the higher-dimensional question. No earlier proof was found as of this review; corrections welcome.

OeisA110566.conjecture.note: The disproof shows 81 (indeed any multiple of 81) never occurs. v_3(a(n)) = floor(log_3 n) + v_3(H(n)). Using the 3-adic splitting H(n) = H(n/3)/3 + (3-integral part) (cf. Shiu, arXiv:1607.02863), the proof shows v_3(H(n)) + log_3 n <= 3 for all n >= 27, and checks 27 <= n < 81 directly. I independently confirmed numerically that max v_3(a(n)) = 3 for n < 3000 and that 27 occurs but 81 does not. The definition matches OEIS (a(1..6) = 1,1,1,1,1,3), and the conjecture (Jianing Song, 2022) is still listed as open in OEIS. The argument is elementary and close to the classical result J_3 = {2,7,22} (Eswarathasan-Levine), but I found no prior record of the refutation. No earlier proof was found as of this review; corrections welcome.

OeisA189409.conjecture_1.note: The statement 'a(n) = (p_n#)^2+1 is always squarefree' is faithful (offset 0, a(0)=2). The disproof is a direct computational counterexample: a(9) = 223092870^2 + 1 = 49770428644836901 = 29^2 * 59180057841661. I verified this independently, and a(0..8) have no square factor below 10^5. The OEIS entry still says it is 'unknown whether or not numbers in this sequence are always squarefree'. Correct and resolves the stated question, though it is a trivial computational observation rather than a deep result. No earlier proof was found as of this review; corrections welcome.

OeisA234360.conjecture_1.note: The proof gives an explicit counterexample n=4722, kernel-checked by rfl without native_decide: certified totients for 1..4721, explicit proper divisors for 4329 values of k, and base-2 Fermat non-witnesses (which validly prove compositeness) for the other 392. So a(4722)=0, refuting Sun's 'a(n)>0 for all n>1'. The definition matches OEIS. OEIS records only Adamczewski's refutation of the other clause of Conjecture (i), the phi/2 - k version at n=1408 (arXiv:2608.11941). That paper does not address a(n)>0, and the b-file stops at n=2500. The first clause, which the formal statement isolates, appears to have been open. No earlier proof was found as of this review; corrections welcome.

OeisA46969.conjecture1.note: The proof establishes the stronger identity a(p) = 12(2p-1) for primes p>3 with 2p-1 prime. It uses von Staudt-Clausen plus Faulhaber/power sums modulo p^2 and q^2 to decide which primes cancel. The conjecture then follows because 2p-1 is prime by hypothesis. The definition (denominator of B_{2n}/(2n(2n-1)), a(1)=12) matches OEIS. The hypotheses (p>3) match 'n>2 in A005382' (p>=7). OEIS still lists Conjecture I as open; only Conjecture II was refuted (Adamczewski). The argument is a classical-style corollary, but I found no prior proof. No earlier proof was found as of this review; corrections welcome.

VCDimConvex.hasAddVCNDimAtMost_two_two_o.note: HasAddVCNDimAtMost C 2 2 means no convex C in R^3 can 2-shatter a 3x3 sumset grid a_i+b_j by translates, and the proof shows exactly that. The steps: shattering forbids opposite-sign convex dependencies, so the direction planes of a and b are distinct 2-planes; a normal form follows; then a covering of R^3 minus 0 by four facial cones forces a convex-combination contradiction between two translates. This is a genuine geometric argument, and the statement is the project's own faithful definition. The problem comes from formal-conjectures itself (section 'What's not in the literature', tagged open), not from an external source. Known neighbours are VC_2 <= 1 false (KitaKen1) and a finite bound of 2^{8(n+2)^n}-1 (KitaKen1). I found no prior proof of the bound 2. No earlier proof was found as of this review; corrections welcome.

OeisA208425.conjecture_2.note: The statement is faithful: a(n) = sum C(n,k)C(n-k,k)C(n+k,k) matches the OEIS formula, and because p = 1 (mod 3) the natural-number divisions 2(p-1)/3 and (p-1)/3 are exact. This is Z.-W. Sun's 2016 conjecture (ii), part 1: sum_{k<p} a(k) = C(2(p-1)/3,(p-1)/3) mod p^2. The proof is a genuine argument. It isolates the exceptional term k=r=(p-1)/3, which yields the binomial coefficient mod p^2, and kills the remaining terms with a finite-field identity, sum over k<=(p-1)/2, k != r, of C(2k,k)/(k-r) = 0 in Z/p. The OEIS entry lists it as a conjecture, and Pan-Sun (Front. Comb. Number Theory 2026, arXiv:2012.05121) prove only part (i). No published proof of (ii) turned up in a search, and the PR cites no prior source. No earlier proof was found as of this review; corrections welcome.

OeisA234360.conjecture_4.note: The target is Sun's conjecture (ii), second part: for n>3, some 0<k<n makes k(k+1)^{phi(n-k)/2}-1 prime. The formalization squares both sides to avoid half-integer exponents. The disproof is a kernel-checked counterexample at n=3998. For 1<=k<=3995 it exhibits an explicit proper divisor or a base-2 Fermat failure of k(k+1)^{phi(3998-k)/2}-1. For k=3996 and 3997, where phi=1, it shows k+1 is not a square, and those two cases also fail under a floor reading (3995 and 3996 are composite), so the counterexample holds under any reasonable reading. Adamczewski (arXiv:2608.11941, the reference in the OEIS comment) disproved only conjecture (i), second part, at n=1408. Formal-conjectures marks that one solved and this one open, so this disproof appears new. It is a modest computational result. No earlier proof was found as of this review; corrections welcome.

OeisA260194.conjecture.note: The definition matches OEIS A260194 (three initial 1s, then a(n+3) = a(n+2) + gcd(a(n+2), a(n)), shifted to index 0), and the question 'does every positive integer occur as a difference?' is rendered exactly. The disproof is a genuine finite modular certificate. It proves that from any state whose last two differences are 1, every later difference is at most 89 until the state returns to (1,1); the sequence enters such a state at its start, so the difference 90 never occurs. OEIS still lists this as an open question, and no prior answer turned up. No earlier proof was found as of this review; corrections welcome.

RefactorableNumber.zelinsky_refactorable.note: The statement is faithful to Zelinsky (J. Integer Seq. 5 (2002), Art. 02.2.8), Conjecture 32: any arithmetic progression of positive integers that contains a tau (refactorable) number contains infinitely many. The formal version is: for every m>=1 and refactorable n0 there is a larger refactorable n with n = n0 mod m. The proof is a real but very short argument: take a prime p > n0 with p = 1 mod m (Dirichlet) and n = n0*p^{p-1}. Then d(n) = d(n0)*p divides n and n = n0 mod m. Wikipedia still lists the question as unsolved, and nothing in OEIS A033950 records a resolution. Caveat: the argument is elementary enough that it may be folklore. No earlier proof was found as of this review; corrections welcome.

Erdos308.erdos_308.variants.all_N.note: The statement (for every N>=1 the representable integers form {1..m}) is the literal Erdős–Graham question 'Let N>=1 ...'. Croot [Cr99] settled it only for sufficiently large N (ineffective o(1)), which is why erdosproblems lists #308 as 'essentially solved'. The proof is a genuine self-contained argument: a kernel-checked base case for N<=64, then an induction showing the maximal representable integer grows by at most 2 per step and that an attained maximum has an attained predecessor. I found no prior all-N proof; Chen's Nov 2026 hexagon preprint covers almost all N only. Caveat: this is a modest strengthening of an already essentially-solved problem. No earlier proof was found as of this review; corrections welcome.

Erdos74.erdos_74.variants.sqrt.note: The statement asks for a graph with infinite chromatic number whose n-vertex subgraphs are all within sqrt(n) edge deletions of bipartite. That matches the problem page's 'open even for f(n)=sqrt n'; the max over (not necessarily induced) subgraphs is the same as over induced ones. The main #74 was disproved by GPT-6 Astra only for a very slowly growing f of order log n/log log n, which does not imply the sqrt(n) case. This self-contained disproof proves that any graph with the sqrt(n) local bound has finite chromatic number, via short odd-walk transversals, shell filtrations and ball-carving colourings. erdosproblems shows no sqrt(n) claim. The proof is credited to @preternatural-tocsin (Gemini agent). No earlier proof was found as of this review; corrections welcome.

OeisA69004.conjecture2.variants.without_.note: The statement (5a(n) >= pi(n) for all n>1, plus three equalities) is exactly T. D. Noe's lower bound with his claimed equalities; the upper half was already refuted at n=512720. The disproof is a genuine unconditional analytic argument. It takes n = 2^r times many primes ≡ 3 (mod 4), bounds a(n) with Selberg's Lambda^2 sieve, uses the divergence of the product of p/(p-1) over p ≡ 3 (mod 4) via finite Euler products, and uses Chebyshev's lower bound for pi(n). It concludes that 5a(n) < pi(n) for some n. I found no prior refutation of the lower bound in OEIS or upstream. Caveat: this is a minor OEIS empirical remark, and the failure was heuristically expected; the proof is non-constructive. No earlier proof was found as of this review; corrections welcome.

OeisA179524.conjecture4.note: The statement n | sum_{k<n} (20k+17) a(k) for all n >= 1, with a(n) = sum_k (-4)^k C(n,k)^2 C(n-k,k)^2 (ℕ subtraction is harmless since k <= n), is exactly Z.-W. Sun's 2010 conjecture as recorded in OEIS A179524. The proof is a genuine argument: a telescoping identity reduces the weight, powers of 2 are handled separately, and for the odd part a q-analogue vanishes at odd-order roots of unity, with cyclotomic specialization giving divisibility. OEIS still lists it as a conjecture, and my searches (Sun's open-conjectures list, follow-up papers) found no prior proof. Caveat: Sun's congruence conjectures are heavily studied, so a prior proof in the literature cannot be fully excluded. No earlier proof was found as of this review; corrections welcome.

OeisA79727.conjecture3.note: The statement a((p^2-1)/2) ≡ p^2 mod p^4 for primes p ≡ 3, 5, 6 mod 7 (OeisA3625.A, with a(n) = sum_{k<=n} C(2k,k)^3) is exactly Peter Bala's Conjecture 3 (July 2024) on OEIS A079727. The proof is a substantial genuine argument: a coefficient of the formal multiplication series of an elliptic curve with CM by Q(sqrt -7), related to a squared Legendre value, plus block cancellation, with p = 3 checked directly. OEIS still lists it as a conjecture (checked up to p = 101), and I found no prior proof. Caveat: the literature search was not exhaustive. No earlier proof was found as of this review; corrections welcome.

VCDimConvex.exists_exponential_bound_has.note: HasAddVCNDimAtMost is the standard VC_n-dimension notion for translates: no (d+1)^n sum-grid is shattered. The statement asks for c >= 2 with bound c^n for every convex set in R^{n+1}. The proof gives c = 3 by proving the stronger bounds VC_n <= 2 for n >= 2 and VC_1 <= 3. It is a long, genuine argument: a self-contained Borsuk-Ulam via Ky Fan parity, convex-position cone arguments and chamber surgery. Upstream marks it open, and the only prior result is Kitamura's doubly exponential bound. Caveat: the conjecture is the formal-conjectures authors' own, with no literature source, and the same author's sibling PRs (#2797, #2823) also claim the sharper open variants. No earlier proof was found as of this review; corrections welcome.

VCDimConvex.hasAddVCNDimAtMost_n_two_of_.note: The Lean statement is exactly the question asked: for all n>=1, every convex set in R^(n+1) has VC_n dimension at most 3, using the standard HasAddVCNDimAtMost definition, which is non-trivial. The proof is a real 4,300-line argument: a Borsuk-Ulam theorem proved from scratch via Ky Fan parity, Radon for n=1, and chamber surgery for n>=3. As a by-product it proves the sharper bound VC_n <= 2 for n >= 2, which also settles the separately listed open lemma hasAddVCNDimAtMost_two_two_of_convex_r3. The PR does not claim to port earlier work. The only prior results I found are Kitamura's finite bound 2^(8(n+2)^n)-1 and his counterexample to <=1, and I found nothing in the literature on this question. Caveat: the question was posed inside formal-conjectures ('What's not in the literature'), not in a published source, and the argument has no human-written exposition. No earlier proof was found as of this review; corrections welcome.

oeis-a262779.note: The formal statement is the conjunction of Colin Barker's two OEIS conjectures for Rule 175 from a single ON cell: a(n) = 101a(n-1) - 100a(n-2) for n > 2, and the g.f. (1+9x+x^2)/((1-x)(1-100x)). Here a(n) is the row of cells -n..n read in base 10, the automaton runs on Z with the rule applied to the background, and the definition reproduces the OEIS data (1, 110, 11011, 1101111, ...). The formalization is faithful; I checked the low-order g.f. coefficients by hand. The proof is genuine. It shows ruleOut 175 = (not l) or r. Induction then shows that for t >= 1 every cell is ON except position 2-t, giving 9a(n) = 10^(2n+1) - 1 - 9*10^(2n-2), from which both claims follow. The entry still lists these as unproved conjectures; OEIS editors in 2022 removed claims that Barker's CA conjectures are proved. I found no earlier proof: A266678 only gives the middle column, and Macfarlane's 2016 paper treats even rule numbers only. Caveat: this is an elementary curve-fit conjecture, not a substantial research problem.

gillibert-equal-halves.note: The formal statement is exactly Gillibert's Equal Halves conjecture (17/11/2026): every finite connected vertex-transitive graph of even order splits as A and its complement, both nonempty, with G[A] and G[Ac] connected and isomorphic. Mathlib's Connected, induce and graph isomorphism are used with no extra hypotheses; the source proves only the Cayley case and leaves the general case open. The disproof exhibits a 28-vertex, 9-regular, non-Cayley vertex-transitive graph (Aut = PSL(2,8), order 504, from the Holt-Royle census). It proves connectivity and vertex-transitivity from explicit automorphisms. An isomorphism of the halves would give a side-swapping involution preserving same-side degree, triangle and distance-2 counts, forcing equal counts of 15 derived predicates on both sides. A kernel-checked bit-plane computation (decide +kernel, no native_decide) shows every balanced 2-colouring violates one of them. This is a real argument, not an encoding exploit. The conjecture is recent and AI-assisted, but it was open at the source, and I found no earlier counterexample. The author's README describes the list as conjectures with nothing known in the literature.

oeis-a263244.note: The formal statement defines the Rule 155 evolution from one ON cell on an OFF background, with every cell updated each step, including the background. It reads cells -n..n as a base-10 digit string. This reproduces the OEIS data (1, 101, 10011, 1011111, ...). It then asserts the conjunction of all conjectured formulas in the entry: Colin Barker's recurrence a(n) = a(n-1) + 10000a(n-2) - 10000a(n-3) for n > 3, his generating function (I checked the coefficients 1, 100, -90, 1100 by hand), and Karl V. Keller's floor formulas for odd and even n. These are exactly the conjectures in the entry, which still labels them as conjectures. The proof is a genuine argument and exploits no loophole: it proves the cell pattern by induction (cell_155_formula), derives closed forms for 9a(n), and from them the step a(n+2) = 10000a(n) + 1111, the recurrence, the power-series identity and the floor formulas. Caveat: this is a routine verification of an empirically fitted formula for a Wolfram class-2 automaton, not a research-level problem. As of this review I found no earlier published proof of these formulas.

mo-236762.note: The MO question (2016, zero answers and no comments as of this review) asks a yes/no question. Let U be a unitary on H = closed span{S_i S_j} in O_infinity that commutes with the flip sigma(S_i S_j) = S_j S_i. Must there be an automorphism of O_infinity that agrees with U on H? The poster suspected NO for U = sigma. The formal statement encodes the YES answer for every C*-algebra generated by a Cuntz family S_i, which by Cuntz uniqueness is O_infinity, with U an inner-product-preserving linear bijection of H commuting with sigma. The disproof proves its negation, so the encoding is faithful. The proof is a genuine argument. If T_i = phi(S_i) were isometries with orthogonal ranges and T_i T_j = S_j S_i, then Q = T_0 T_0^* would satisfy x_N S_0 = S_0 and x_N S_1 = 0, where x_N = S_N^* Q S_N. But on the dense *-algebra spanned by the words S_mu S_nu^*, the compression S_N^* w S_N is eventually a scalar. Approximating Q within 1/3 then gives a contradiction. A concrete model on l^2(N) supplies a nonzero algebra and the flip operator. I found no earlier answer or reference settling this. Caveat: this answers a modest MO question, not a named conjecture, and leaves the poster's follow-up request for a characterisation untouched.

oeis-a346644.note: The formal statement says that every n > 0 is the reduced denominator of sigma(k)/tau(k) for some k > 0, where divisorMean(k) is the rational sum of divisors over number of divisors and Rat.den is the reduced denominator. This is exactly the OEIS conjecture 'k always exists'. The proof is a genuine explicit construction. Write n = 2^v u with u odd, G = 2^(2^v) - 1 and M = uG. Dirichlet's theorem (Mathlib's Nat.forall_exists_prime_gt_and_modEq) gives a prime p = -1 mod 2M. For k = 2^(2^v - 1) p^(M-1), tau(k) = nG and sigma(k) = G(1 + p + ... + p^(M-1)), and the geometric sum is 1 mod 2M, so the reduced denominator is exactly n. I checked the argument and it is correct. The OEIS entry, the related entries A057020 and A057021, and the Bateman-Erdos-Pomerance-Straus paper on the arithmetic mean of divisors contain no proof, and a web search found none. Caveat: the argument is elementary.

oeis-a354478.note: The statement defines rowSum n = Sum_{k=1..n} 1/s(n,k) with signed Stirling numbers of the first kind. This matches Mathematica StirlingS1 and the OEIS data: n=2 gives 0, n=3 gives 7/6. It asserts num/den of rowSum n -> 1, which is exactly Kotesovec's conjecture 'a(n)/A354479(n) tends to 1' (Jun 2022), and the entry still marks it as a conjecture. The proof is a genuine elementary argument. It proves by induction on the Stirling recurrence that n(n-1) <= 2|s(n,k)| for 1 <= k < n and n >= 4, so the n-1 off-diagonal terms contribute at most 2/n while the diagonal term is 1; it exploits no encoding artefact. Neither A354478, A354479 nor a web search turned up an earlier written proof as of this review. Caveat: the result is easy (essentially |s(n,k)| >= C(n,2) off the diagonal), so it is a valid but very minor settlement of an OEIS remark.

oeis-a263245.note: The statement defines Rule 155 from a single ON cell. The rule is applied to the background too, so the background turns ON after step 1, as in the OEIS data. Cells -n..n are read in base 2, and I checked that this reproduces all 1001 b-file terms. It states the conjunction of Colin Barker's conjectured recurrence and g.f. with Karl V. Keller's odd and even closed forms (the ℤ-division exponents are exact under the parity hypotheses), so it faithfully captures the conjectures in the entry. Barker's separate 'Empirical' formula is omitted, but it follows from the g.f. The proof is a genuine induction. It shows that for t ≥ 1 the row is all ON except at position 1-t (odd t), or except at positions 1-t and 2-t (even t). From this it computes a(n) = 3*2^(2n-1) - 1 and 5*2^(2n-2) - 1, then a(n+2) = 16a(n) + 15, and derives the recurrence and g.f. coefficientwise. It uses no native_decide or other tricks. A263245 and its companions A263243/A263244 still label all these formulas as conjectures or empirical, and I found no earlier proof as of this review. The result is mathematically routine (a trivially eventually-periodic automaton), so it is a confirmation of an OEIS-level conjecture, not a significant open problem.

oeis-a379181.note: The source conjecture (Stefano Spezia, Jul 23 2025) is 'a(n+1)/a(n) ~ 10', i.e. the ratio tends to 10; the formal statement is exactly Tendsto (term(n+1)/term(n)) atTop (nhds 10), and the disproof proves its negation. term(n) counts k < 10^n with exactly n digits (0 counted for n=1, so term 1 = 10) whose digit multiset has a unique mode m equal to the mean (sum = m*n), matching the OEIS definition and the Mathematica code Commonest==={Mean}; the n=0 term (0, giving ratio 0 in Lean) does not affect the limit. The proof is a genuine argument: the mean must be an integer, hence at distance >= 1/2 from 4.5, and a digit-flip symmetry plus an exponential-moment (Chernoff-type) bound gives term(n) <= 2*(9.9)^n, whereas a ratio tending to 10 would force term(N+r) >= 9.95^r*term(N), a contradiction via Bernoulli's inequality. The current OEIS entry (rev #27) still lists the conjecture with no refutation, so this disproof is new. The true growth rate is a constrained large-deviation constant strictly below 10, which is consistent with the listed terms (ratios ~9.1-9.6).

oeis-a292727.note: The move relation matches the entry: you pick two equal piles x,x, move 1<=y<=x stones, and drop an emptied pile. a(n) is the number of positive partitions of n not reachable from 1^n. The statement indexes from n>=1 and agrees with the data (a(10)=4 with the listed unreachable states; a(12)=7, a(24)=26, a(20)=9, a(40)=30, a(28)=11, a(56)=34). The two iff conjectures (a(n)=0 iff n is a power of 2, a(n)=1 iff n is an odd prime) are not new: Charlie Neder proved both in the companion entry A292726 (Jan 2019, 'both conjectures are true'), and the proof uses the same odd-divisor invariant. The new part is the pair of formulas a(4p)=p+4 and a(8p)=2p+20, which A292727 still gives only as Neder's conjecture; no proof turned up in a search. The proof derives them from its own lemmas, not by computation for particular p (the only decide calls are partition counts for 4 and 8): reachable_of_pow_two_mul_prime, explicit counts of odd pairs not divisible by p, and ncard_mul_prime. I confirm it on the strength of those two formulas; the iff parts should be credited to Neder.

oeis-a309417.note: A309417 (Moewald, 2019) conjectures that lim a(n+1)/a(n) = 10, where a(n) is the number of steps from 10^n to 0 under x -> x - digitsum(x). term n = countSteps(10^n)(10^n), and the fuel 10^n is enough because each step strictly decreases a positive x. This gives term 1 = 2, matching a(1)=2. Including the extra index n=0 (term 0 = 1) does not change the limit, and term n > 0 is proved, so the real ratio is well defined. The proof is a genuine second-moment argument. The orbit from 10^n visits distinct numbers below 10^n whose digit sums add up to exactly 10^n. Exact second-moment and bounded fourth-moment computations for the digit sum over [0,10^n) show that few numbers have digit sum far from 4.5n. Together these give term n ~ 10^n/(4.5n), so the ratio tends to 10. The entry still lists it as a conjecture with no proof, and a web search found no earlier proof.

oeis-a108629.note: The statement encodes the g.f. (1+x-sqrt(1-2x-3x^2-4x^3))/(2+2x+2x^2) over Q, taking the square-root branch with constant term 1 via binomialSeries(1/2) composed with -2X-3X^2-4X^3. With a(n) = coeff n, a(0)=0 and a(1)=1, which matches OEIS offset 1 (1,0,1,2,4,11,...). The recurrence is exactly R. J. Mathar's 'Conjecture D-finite with recurrence' (Jan 2020), stated for n>=6 where every index is defined; I checked it by hand at n=6 (66=66). The proof is a genuine algebraic derivation. It uses R^2 = 1+t to get 2(1+t)R' = t'R, substitutes R = 1+X-2(1+X+X^2)A to get a first-order linear ODE for A, and reads off coefficients. The entry still marks the recurrence as conjectural. The result is routine (any algebraic g.f. is D-finite), so its novelty is low, but no earlier proof exists in the source.

mo-348551.note: The question (no answers; only David Handelman's comment that it is unlikely to be tractable) asks to show that phi_i(k) = (lambda_i - lambda_{i+1})/k is unimodal, where lambda_j are the ordered eigenvalues of (A^T)^k A^k / rho(A)^{2k} and A is any entrywise nonnegative matrix. The formalisation is faithful: it requires positive Perron root (needed for the division, and noted in the comments), lists eigenvalues with multiplicity in decreasing order, uses k>0, and defines unimodality as nondecreasing up to k0 and nonincreasing after, which matches the source's definition. The disproof uses A = [1] (+) [[0,1],[1/4,0]] with rho=1. At even times the normalized Gram matrix is diag(1,16^-m,16^-m); at odd times it is diag(1,16^-m/16,16^-m) up to order. So phi_2 alternates between 0 and a positive value and cannot be unimodal for any k0, under the MO definition as well. The 2x2 irreducible block alone already gives a counterexample, so nonnegative matrices are definitely not unimodal in general. The argument is genuine and elementary. The only caveat is that the asker might have meant primitive matrices, but did not say so.

oeis-a229623.note: The OEIS entry gives the data 0,1,...,9,11,101,...,929,1001,10001,... with offset 1, and Derek Orr's 2015 conjecture a(n) = 10^(n-18)+1 for n>20. The statement uses Nat.nth qualifies (n-1) with qualifies m := digits(m) palindrome and digits(m - digitsum m) palindrome, which matches: nth 0 = 0 and the 21st term is 1001 = 10^3+1. Range n>=21 is correct and there is no weakening. The proof is a real digit argument. For an L-digit palindrome m >= 10^4 the digit sum s < 10^(L/2). If m-s loses a digit, then m = 10^(L-1)+1. If the top half is unchanged, mirroring forces 10^(L/2) | s, which is impossible. Otherwise a borrow forces s = 10^q mod 10^(q+1) with s <= 18(q+1), also impossible. The finite range below 10^4 is checked with decide. Neither the entry nor A229621 marks the conjecture as proved, and I found no earlier proof.

arxiv-2404.06445.note: Conjecture 8.9 ('Main Conjecture') of Mallik, Diwan and Kothari v3 says that every minimal k-extendable bipartite graph has |V_{k+1}| ≥ 2/(2k-1)·(m - n + 2k). The formal statement matches the paper's Section 8 definitions: connected, order ≥ 2k+2, has a k-matching, every k-matching extends to a perfect matching, minimal under edge deletion, V_{k+1} = vertices of degree exactly k+1, no extra order threshold. The disproof is an explicit 16-vertex bipartite graph with k = 3. H_A–L_B and L_A–H_B are complete (|H| = 3, |L| = 5), plus a perfect matching between L_A and L_B and one edge between H_A and H_B, for m = 36 and only 10 vertices of degree 4, below the bound 52/5 = 10.4. I checked this independently by brute force: the graph is connected and bipartite, every 3-matching extends to a perfect matching, every single-edge deletion destroys 3-extendability, and it is consistent with Lou's theorem and with the paper's Conjecture 8.10 (tight at 10). It does not use small-order degeneracy, since n = 16 ≥ 8. I found no earlier counterexample: the only later paper on these bounds (He, arXiv 2611.29504, confirming Conjecture 8.11 for k ≥ 3) does not address 8.9.

oeis-a122251.note: The formal statement matches Paul Barry's 2006 general conjecture. For every prime p and every n, the reduced numerator of det[1/(1+p(i+j))] over 0≤i,j≤n equals (p^2)^{sum_{k=1..n} sum_{j=0..n} floor(k/p^j)}. I checked n=1, p=3: det = 9/112. The companion entry A122249 (p=2) still says 'Conjecture - requires proof', and I found no proof in the OEIS or in the literature I searched; arXiv 2607.18644 handles different Barry conjectures. The proof is a genuine argument. It eliminates the last pivot to get det_{t+1} = det_t·(p^t t!/prod_i(1+p(i+t)))^2/(1+2pt). It then uses a classical divisibility fact: the part of t! coprime to p divides the product of t consecutive terms of an arithmetic progression with step p. So the denominator is coprime to p and the numerator is exactly p^{2(t+v_p(t!))} at each step, which sums to the conjectured exponent. The argument is elementary, but I found no earlier source for it.

oeis-a401159.note: T(n,m) is formalised as the number of labelled Bool-matrices on Fin n x Fin m with at most two trues per row and per column. The two conjectures (Mathar, Nov 18 2026) appear as T(n,2) = A086601(n) = (1+n+C(n,2))^2 and 8T(n,3) = 8+8n+22n^2+13n^3+n^4+3n^5+n^6. These match the entry: A086601 = A000124^2, the denominator 8 is cleared, and the restriction to n≥m is the triangle's own domain. The T(n,2) half is close to trivial, because a row of length 2 can never break its limit, so the two columns are independent subsets of size at most 2. The proof says exactly this. For T(n,3) the proof uses inclusion-exclusion over the triples of column-sets whose common intersection is nonempty, and derives T + n·n^3 = (1+n+C(n,2))^3 + C(n,2). Mathar's 2014 paper only tabulates the values and gives no closed forms. The entry is new and labels both formulas as conjectures, so this is a correct and faithful proof of two easy but recent conjectures; I found no earlier source.

oeis-a057663.note: The statement is faithful to Gerasimov's 2019 conjecture: for k≥1, φ(k+2^k) = φ(k)+2^k holds exactly when k and k+2^k are both prime. The k≥1 restriction matches a sequence of positive integers. I found no other OEIS entry that mentions the identity, and A057663 still calls it a conjecture. The proof is genuine and elementary. Suppose N = k+2^k is composite with least prime factor p. Then N - φ(N) ≥ N/p ≥ sqrt(N) ≥ k, using k^2 ≤ k+2^k. That contradicts N - φ(N) = k - φ(k) < k. Hence N is prime, so φ(k) = k-1, which forces k to be prime. The conjecture is easy, but no earlier proof was found.

mo-309804.note: The formal statement is faithful. A is real upper triangular with negative diagonal, so it is Hurwitz with real spectrum. X and P are symmetric positive definite (Mathlib PosDef includes symmetry), tr X = 1, AP+PA^T = -X, and the objective is tr(X(I+P)^{-1}). The set of values is nonempty and bounded by 1, so Lean's sSup convention cannot trivialise the claim, and the target 2trA/(2trA-1) lies in (0,1). On MathOverflow the question has only two partial answers (an orthogonal-invariance remark and first-order conditions) and comments, none of which settles it. The proof is a genuine argument. Using tr(XP^{-1}) = -2trA, a Kakutani fixed-point step (Brouwer/Kakutani code adapted from harfe's MIT repository, with attribution) gives a PSD trace-one state supported on a single eigenspace of P, whose eigenvalue c must equal -1/(2trA). That state attains 1/(1+c) = 2trA/(2trA-1), and a regularisation step approaches it from the positive definite side. The proof also gives the reverse inequality through a tangent bound, so it establishes the asker's numerically observed equality. I found no earlier solution.

oeis-a033955.note: The statement is faithful to Alonso del Arte's conjecture (Jul 27 2026): for n>6 (1-based), the sum of prime(n) mod prime(k) over k<n exceeds prime(n). With the zero-based Nat.nth, 5<n is exactly the 1-based n>6, and the sum runs over the n smaller primes. The bound is strict and the threshold is correct, since a(6)=13=prime(6). The conjecture is recent and the entry gives no proof. The proof is genuine. For p ≥ 65536 it uses Mathlib's Chebyshev theta bounds to show that the primes in (p/3, p) contribute enough remainder. It then checks 256 ≤ p < 65536 with kernel-verified block certificates and 17 ≤ p < 256 with explicit rows.

oeis-a283508.note: The formal model follows the entry's Mathematica program. The rule bit is selected at index centre + 2·(von Neumann neighbour count) in 643, all cells of the infinite grid update, the origin is read first through (n,0) as decimal digits, and Rule 187 is used for A267623. The statement packages all four empirical conjectures: Barker's generating function, closed form and recurrence, and Mathar's a(n) = A267623(n). The proof is a genuine, if easy, argument. Rule 643 turns on cells that have no ON neighbours, so after two steps the grid reaches a fixed pattern in which every cell is ON except the 8 around the origin. Rule 187 sends the single ON cell to a moving 'hole' row. Both give the digit string 1,0,1,1,1,..., and the three formulas follow. The entry still labels these as conjectures and I found no earlier written proof, so I confirm it, while noting that the content is a routine calculation.

OeisA113258.conjecture.note: The DeepMind statement defines a n = sum_{i<n} (i+1)!^((n-i)!), which equals the OEIS formula sum_{i=1..n} (i!)^((n-i+1)!). It asks for some n > 4, b > 1, e > 1 with a n = b^e, which is exactly Vos Post's question 'Is there a nontrivial power after a(4) = 5^3?'. The disproof shows no later term is a perfect power. This is a substantial argument of about 7400 lines with no sorry and no custom axiom (CI audits axioms). It shows: (1) 2^((n-1)!) < a(n) < 2^((n-1)!) + 2^(4(n-2)!), so any exponent prime p must satisfy p >= n; (2) explicit prime-modulus witnesses rule out n = 5..8 and every (n,p) in the remaining finite range; (3) a formalised special case of Laurent's lower bound for linear forms in two logarithms (interpolation-determinant proof, `LaurentTwoLog`, `direct_log_bound`) bounds p for large n. I found no earlier resolution. The OEIS entry still asks the question, and all four Epoch OEIS-Open runs on this problem (OpenAI, GDM, Anthropic, Gemini) scored I (incorrect). This looks like a genuine new result, not a weakening.

oeis-a214074.note: The statement faithfully encodes Kimberling's 2012 conjecture: for n >= 1, the least m > 0 with gcd(2^n - m, 3^n - m) = 1 is 3 if and only if n = 330k - 209 for some k >= 1. The integer gcd handles negative values correctly. The disproof takes n = 3438721 = 330*10421 - 209. Modulo the prime 487891, both 2^n and 3^n are 3; I re-checked this independently, and 487891 has no divisor below its square root. So 487891 divides gcd(2^n - 3, 3^n - 3), 3 is not in the set, and the 'if' direction fails; the exponent progression 3438721 + 5366790t gives infinitely many counterexamples. This is a genuine, non-trivial counterexample: the exhibited counterexample n ≈ 3.4 million lies far beyond the 1000-term b-file, and finding it needs a search for a prime obstruction of this size. The OEIS entry and the related entries (A214180, A214707-A214709) still list the conjecture unrefuted. Neither the Epoch OEIS-Open paper nor Fried's 2026 OEIS-conjecture paper mentions A214074. I found no earlier refutation.

OeisA79727.conjecture2.note: The statement is that a(p(p-1)) = p^2 mod p^3 for primes p = 3, 5, 6 mod 7 (OeisA3625.A), with a(n) = sum_{k<=n} C(2k,k)^3. This is exactly Peter Bala's Conjecture 2 (July 2024) on OEIS A079727, which still lists it as a conjecture. I checked numerically that it holds for p = 3, 5, 13, 17, 19. The proof (about 3960 lines, no sorry or native_decide, with p=3 done separately) is a substantial original argument. It expands a(p(p-1)) mod p^3 in blocks and uses the supersingular CM curve y^2 = (x+21)(x^2+7) (Hasse invariant), a 2-isogeny and Picard-Fuchs/Wronskian identities. It is in the same family as the already-confirmed OeisA79727.conjecture3. Searches found only Zhi-Hong Sun's mod p^2 result for a(p-1) and unrelated mod p^3 supercongruences (e.g. arXiv:2408.09776, arXiv:2610.34160), no proof of this congruence. No earlier proof was found as of this review; corrections welcome.

OeisA157237.conjecture.note: The definition matches OEIS: a(n) counts (x,y), x,y>=1, with 2n-1-2^x-11*2^y prime and ≡ 1 (mod 6). The Lean 'iff' statement is Sun's conjecture exactly. The disproof is an explicit counterexample n=333811606269876, i.e. 2n-1 = 667623212539751, with every candidate difference shown ≡/≡ 1 mod 6 or given an explicit proper divisor. I independently checked that all 549 differences ≡ 1 (mod 6) are composite, so a(n)=0, and n is not one of the listed exceptions. OEIS records only verification below 1.5*10^8 and no counterexample, and searches found no earlier record of this number or a refutation. No earlier proof was found as of this review; corrections welcome.

Erdos473.erdos_473.variants.finite.note: The statement (for every n >= 2 there is a permutation of {1..n}, via Fin n ≃ Fin n shifted by 1, with all adjacent sums prime) is exactly Segal's finite question on erdosproblems.com/473. The page says it is open and 'true for infinitely many n' via bounded prime gaps; van Doorn in the forum knew no proof. The closest prior work is Y.-F. She (arXiv:2609.19114, 16 Sep 2026), who proves that prime circles of order 2n exist for all sufficiently large n. That would give the path version for all large n, but with an ineffective n0, so the all-n statement was not established. OEIS A051252 still says there is no proof for all n. The 10.6k-line proof is fully effective: strong induction with reflection primes, explicit prime counts in (33N/34, N] for N >= 9.1*10^19 via a certified sieve, and certified small cases. No sorry or axioms. No earlier complete proof was found as of this review; corrections welcome.

RudinsConjecture.rudins_conjecture_uniqu.reason: The formal 'uniqueness' says that for all N>=6 every non-trivial progression attaining Qmax(N) has difference exactly 24. At N=6 the progression 120n+49 (49, 169, 289, 529) attains Q(6)=4, which refutes that claim trivially. The literature 'super-strong' conjecture of González-Jiménez–Xarles asserts uniqueness only up to equivalence and only for N = GP_k + 1 >= 8, so the formalization (all N>=6, literal q=24) is stronger than the real conjecture. The disproof exploits this mismatch and says nothing about the actual conjecture.

Bugeaud06.problem_10_6_variant_1.reason: The proof is a genuine, elementary construction: m enumerates {a*2^t : 1 <= a <= floor(log t)+1}. Density for every irrational xi follows from Dirichlet's theorem plus doubling, and consecutive ratios are >= 1 + (1/2)/log n. But Bugeaud's Problem 10.6 ('find a very rapidly increasing sequence...') is open-ended and not a precise statement. 'IsGenuinelySublacunary' (ratio floor 1 + c/log n, i.e. growth only about exp(cn/log n)) is a threshold the formalizers chose themselves, and the same argument works with any unbounded multiplier bound A(t). So it is not what Bugeaud asks, and proving it does not solve Problem 10.6. At most it settles a weak, catalogue-invented variant.

Green44.green_44.reason: The disproof only works because the formalization quantifies over all N, with no 'N sufficiently large' condition. It takes N = 100000 and the 1000 primes in [20011, 30161], which are < N^{9/10} = 31622 only because N^{1/10} < 10. Each A_i is the block of residues 10002..10001 + floor(p_i/2), so all of [1, 10001] survives and 10*|remaining| = 100010 > N. For large N (any N > 10^10) every prime is below N/10, and this trivial block trick is impossible. Green's question (from Erdős, contrasting with the large-sieve range p < N^{1/2}) is about the asymptotic regime, so nothing was learned about the real problem.

Erdos354.erdos_354.parts.ii.reason: The formal statement reads 'what if 2 is replaced by some gamma in (1,2)' as an EXISTENTIAL over gamma. The proof (a port of Kenta Kitamura's development) just picks gamma = sqrt(golden ratio) and shows that a SINGLE floor sequence floor(gamma^n alpha) is complete for every alpha>0. The second sequence and the hypothesis that alpha/beta is irrational are never used, which shows the formalization has removed the actual content of the question (whether, or for which, gamma in (1,2) the two-sequence statement holds as it does for gamma=2). This does not answer the question as erdosproblems.com poses it.

mo-93022.reason: The formal statement takes literally the question's 'that is' clause: v is connecting if for all p != q some k > 0 gives p.v^k = q or q.v^k = p. It then asks for such a v of length <= n-1 whenever one exists. The disproof is a 5-state, 3-letter automaton with a reset letter, checked by decide. It has a connecting word of length 6, and every word of length <= 4 is constant or preserves a nontrivial 2-colouring. Under that literal reading the counterexample is valid. However, the question is not precise or self-consistent. It asks about words whose 'underlying graph is connected' (Berlinkov's one-cluster setting), and in the comments the author says one may also assume that w takes A into one state. A constant map is never connecting in the literal sense once n >= 3, so the literal clause cannot be what was meant. A commenter also notes that assumptions are missing, which makes the answer obviously 'no'. Under the graph-connectivity reading the counterexample fails: its length-1 reset letter has a connected (one-cluster) functional graph. So the disproof settles a literal reading the author's own clarifications contradict, not a precise open question.

Erdos40.erdos_40.reason: The upstream erdos_40 is a 'question value' statement: {g | g -> infinity and Erdos40For g} = erdos_40.answer, where answer is a sorry placeholder. The PR proves only that this holds if answer is replaced by its own OMA.answer. OMA.answer is {g | g -> infinity and for all k there is T >= k such that every p in maximalProfiles k T violates a finite inequality against sqrt(i)/g(i)}. The proof gets there by rewriting with erdos40For_iff_finite (a compactness truncation to finite sets with representation count <= k) and finite_iff_profile_obstruction. So the 'answer' is a mechanical restatement of the defining predicate Erdos40For through finite truncations, not an explicit characterisation of the admissible g. The file header admits that the criterion 'does not settle whether there is any divergent denominator satisfying it', so it does not even settle the weaker variant or Erdős #28. The extra side results (log-band and fourth-root counterexamples) are partial and are not the stated problem. erdosproblems.com still lists #40 as open with 0 proof claims; this is a trivialised answer, not a solution.

mo-407245.reason: The MO question asks for the smallest l (as a function of k,n, or even an asymptotic bound) such that any l equipartitions of a kn-set force a pair to share a block in at least half of them. The formal statement does not give an answer: it defines threshold k n through hasOrthogonal k n 3 and hasOrthogonal k n 4, which are brute-force `decide` searches over every family of partitions, and only proves that the minimum is 3, 4 or nonexistent depending on those uncomputed predicates. The proof is the easy reduction: a pair that meets at most once can't reach r/2 for r=3,4, and repeating 4 pairwise orthogonal equipartitions cyclically defeats every r >= 3. Peter Taylor's comment under the question already gives this repetition idea (using Kirkman's 7 orthogonal partitions). The real content, namely for which (k,n) 3 or 4 mutually orthogonal equipartitions exist (for k=n this is the existence of 1 or 2 MOLS of order n, so e.g. k=n=6 gives 4), is left undetermined. The theorem therefore restates the question in terms of an unsolved design-existence predicate rather than settling it.

mo-148821.reason: The MathOverflow question (no answers, no comments) is open-ended: 'what can we say about |M_1 ∪ ... ∪ M_b| compared to a maximum b-matching, is anything known about the ratio?'. It gives no precise conjecture or candidate value, and the statement file says so itself. The formal 'answer' does not compute the ratio. It proves that p/q is guaranteed iff a finite integer certificate exists (`certified b p q`: labels, weights and linear inequalities over subsets of Fin b). That is an LP-duality/blow-up characterisation, which in effect restates the question as a finite linear program. It gives no explicit bound, does not even recover the 1/2 the asker noted for b = 1, 2, and says nothing about how the ratio behaves as b grows. The Lean proof (Farkas lemma plus a blow-up construction realising the dual) is a real argument, and legalRounds does faithfully encode successive maximal matchings. But it does not settle the source question, which is not a precise yes/no problem.

oeis-a346214.reason: The disproof attacks only the second conjunct, the finite formula T(n,n-j) = A002884(n)/(A002884(j)·2^(n-(j-1)^2)), stated 'for j < 2n'. It refutes that at n = 2, j = 1, where T(2,1) = 1 but the formula gives 6/4. The range 'j < 2n' is plainly a typo by Critzer: it allows every j < n, and the formula already fails at n = 3, j = 2 (1 vs 14) and at n = 4, j = 2 (315 vs 420). It holds in the checked cases with 2j < n (n = 3, j = 1: 21; n = 4, j = 1: 1260; n = 5, j = 2: 104160), so the intended statement is evidently 'for n > 2j'. The formalisation copied the typo literally, and the counterexample exploits only that. The actual conjecture is the limiting distribution lim P(X_n = j) = ∏(1-2^-i)·2^((j-1)^2)/A002884(j), together with the corrected finite formula, and the PR does not touch it. So the conjecture has not really been refuted.

oeis-a124352.reason: Barker's g.f./recurrence conjecture (and Mathar's equivalent form) is still marked as a conjecture in A124352 and A307933. The proof is a genuine 117-state transfer-matrix argument. However, the formal statement never mentions the antiprism or Hamiltonian paths. `a n` is defined as the output of an agent-written frontier/connectivity dynamic program (masks, addEdge, forget, closing), and the only link to the OEIS quantity is a docstring claim. The real mathematical step, that this program counts directed Hamiltonian paths of C_{2n}^2, is assumed rather than proved. Given the program, the recurrence is just Cayley-Hamilton bookkeeping. I ported the program to Python and it matches brute-force counts for n = 3..6 (240, 816, 2400, 6480) and the data up to n = 13, so it is very likely correct. But the Lean theorem does not certify the conjecture as stated: it proves a property of a custom algorithm, which is a degenerate encoding unless that algorithm is formally tied to the graph count.

Erdos691.erdos_691.note: Erdos asks for 'a necessary and sufficient condition' on A for M_A to have density 1, which is an open-ended request. The formal statement erdos_691.answer = (fun A => (multiples A).HasDensity 1) is satisfied by the tautological answer. So it accepts any equivalent predicate and cannot tell a real answer from a restatement. The submitted OMA.answer says that A meets every 'AdmissibleTest'. A test is an arbitrary infinite sequence of finite divisor-closed sets on prime blocks satisfying a harmonic-mass retention inequality, so the criterion quantifies over an uncountable family of obstruction certificates. It is a dual reformulation of the Behrend property, not an arithmetic condition on A. The forum thread notes that the analogous finite-approximation criterion is the classical Davenport-Erdos fact (Hall-Tenenbaum (1.3)) and does not count as a solution. The file says it is a port of github.com/Ghuffy1/erdos691, and erdosproblems.com/691 remains open. The proof is valid but does not solve the problem as posed.

Erdos357.erdos_357.parts.ii.bigO_version.note: The question is 'how does f(n) grow / find a good explicit g with f = O(g)'. The real open problem is whether f(n) = o(n). The formal statement f =O[atTop] answer is trivially satisfied by answer(n) = n, since a strictly increasing sequence in [1,n] has at most n terms. So it is vacuous. The submitted answer (44273/90000)n + 2 sqrt n + 177792 is again linear, so the Big-O conclusion carries no information beyond the trivial bound; the sharper constant (about 0.4919 < 1/2, said to be from Chandler Snively's 2026 preprint) is invisible to the statement. Known upper bounds on the page and forum are (2/3 - 1/512)n (Coppersmith-Phillips), about 0.8727n (Beker), and a claimed n/2 + O(n^{2/3}) (Lenthall-Cleary, July 2026). The PR itself concedes that 'whether f(n)=o(n) remains open'. Not a solution.

Erdos692.erdos_692.parts.ii.note: Erdos asks where, for fixed n, delta_1(n,m) attains its maximum. The formal statement only requires some function answer(n) at which the maximum over m > n+1 is attained. The submitted OMA.answer(n) is literally the argmax of the exact density, computed as residue counts mod m!, over the candidates m in [n+2, n+2+A+B], where A = (3^{2(n+1)^2})! and B is a factorial of a factorial. This is a brute-force argmax of the very quantity asked about, with a tower-type cutoff. It proves that the maximum exists and is attained below an astronomically large bound, but it gives no information about where the maximum lies, which is what Erdos asked; the PR concedes 'the cutoff is too large for practical computation'. erdosproblems.com/692 (Cambie: superpolynomially many local maxima) gives no closed form, and the question remains open.

Erdos732.erdos_732.parts.i.note: Erdos asks whether there are reasonable necessary and sufficient conditions for a sequence (X_i) to be block-compatible, i.e. realizable as the block sizes of a pairwise balanced design. The formal 'question value' statement accepts any predicate equivalent to membership in blockSizeProfiles n. The submitted OMA.answer says that s is sorted and that a coefficient of prod over all T subset of [n] with |T|>=2 of (1 + x^{term T}) is positive. By the proof's own lemma coeff_pos, that coefficient is positive iff there is a family of blocks covering every pair exactly once with the size multiset s. So it is the definition of block-compatibility re-encoded as a generating function, i.e. exhaustive search. The PR says 'this criterion makes no efficiency claim'. This is a restatement, not a solution.

Erdos1017.erdos_1017.upper_bound.note: Erdős asks to 'estimate' (sharpen) the clique-partition number f(n,k) for k > n^2/4. The formal 'upper_bound' only asks for some function with f(n,k) <= answer(n,k). Any known bound satisfies it: the API lemma f <= k, or Erdős–Goodman–Pósa's n^2/4. The supplied OMA.answer is min(n^2/4, k - C(r,2) + 1) with r = n - (C(n,2)-k). That is EGP plus the elementary bound 'a clique on n-q vertices, then the remaining edges one by one'. No matching lower bound and no asymptotic estimate is given. The one-sided statement is essentially vacuous as a formalization of the problem, so problem 1017 is not solved.

Erdos422.erdos_422.variants.growth_rate.note: 'How does f grow?' for Hofstadter's Q-sequence is formalized only as a one-sided bound f =O(answer), with answer supplied by the solver. OMA.answer = n, and the proof is f(n) <= n, which is built into the IsHofstadterQ predicate itself (it requires f(n-1) < n so that the recurrence is defined). The file also proves f(n) > c n infinitely often for c < 1/2, but the solution does not use it, and neither describes the actual growth (conjecturally f(n) ≈ n/2 with chaotic fluctuations). It is not even known that f is defined for all n. The answer is the trivial bound, so nothing about problem 422 is settled.

Erdos450.erdos_450.note: Erdős asks how large y(eps,n) must be, i.e. for an estimate of the threshold's size; the page discusses regimes such as y ~ 2n for eps << 1/n and no finite y at all for larger eps. The formal statement asks for exact equality windowThreshold eps n = answer eps n with an unconstrained answer function. The proof's OMA.answer is just a finite sup over residues x, r modulo P = lcm(n+1,...,2n-1) of a 'cutoff' solving the periodic counting inequality, i.e. the definition of the threshold re-expressed as a brute-force computation over one period. This proves only that the threshold is computable from periodicity and says nothing about how y(eps,n) grows in eps and n. The formalisation admits this tautological answer, so the open problem is not solved.

Arxiv.2507.17780.tx_graffiti_conjecture_.reason: This disproof uses a real counterexample: an explicit 50-vertex cubic graph with a maximal matching of 15 edges (every edge meets vertices 0..29), and a kernel-checked certificate that no independent dominating set has 15 or fewer vertices. So i(G)=16 > 15 >= mu*(G). The definitions (IsIndepDominating, IsMaximalEdgeMatching) are faithful. However, this 50-vertex graph with i(G)=16 > 15 = gamma_e(G) was already published as a counterexample to the TxGraffiti i(G) <= mu*(G) conjecture: a Zenodo release in 2026 (doi:10.5281/zenodo.21852504), cited by Afrasyab, arXiv:2609.10783 (Sep 2026), whose abstract states it 'had been used to refute the stronger independent-domination inequality'. The upstream 'open' tag is out of date.

Erdos18.erdos_18a.reason: The formal statement matches the first ($250) question: there exist infinitely many practical m with h(m) < (log log m)^C. The proof is a real sieve/Fourier argument, but its own header says it follows Wouter van Doorn and GPT-6 Astra Pro (github.com/Woett/ChatGPT-s-note-on-Erdos18), building on Liam Price. Both are public proof claims on erdosproblems.com/18: Price, 2026-07-24, h(n) << (log log n)^2; van Doorn, 2026-09-16, with a full Lean formalisation. So this is a re-formalisation of an already-claimed result, not a new one.

Erdos252.erdos_252.variants.k_ge_five.reason: The file proves irrationality of sum sigma_k(n)/n! for every k, specialised to k>=5. The argument is real: factorial tails become integers under rationality, a Stirling expansion, and CRT-aligned dilations giving unequal progression means. The file states it is adapted from github.com/tokengr1nder/Erdos252. oeis-a183761.reason: Kimberling's 2012 conjecture says the count of nonsingular 0..n 2x2 matrices with lexicographically increasing rows equals the count of 0..n matrices with positive determinant. The Lean proof is exactly Radcliffe's argument: the row swap is an involution that negates the determinant and reverses the row order, and nonsingular matrices have distinct rows. It is correct but already proved in the entry.

oeis-a168670.reason: The formal statement matches the OEIS comment: for n>1 with n%11 in {1,8}, 36n^2+72n+35 is never p(p+2) with p and p+2 both prime. The proof just replays this argument, so this is not a new result.

oeis-a292728.reason: The formalisation is faithful. A move picks two equal piles x and sends 1 <= y <= x stones between them; an emptied pile is dropped. The proof is genuine: a backward invariant (if every pile after a move is divisible by an odd d, so was every pile before it) makes [n] and pairs of odd parts unreachable; explicit constructions reach every distinct partition when n = 2^k, and every one except [p] when n is an odd prime. However, the substantive directions were already recorded in the companion entry A292727 (unreachable states, same game). There Charlie Neder (Jan 26 2019) gives as formulas, not conjectures, 'a(2^k) = 0' and 'for p an odd prime, a(p) = 1' (and a(2p) = (p+3)/2). These say every state, terminal ones included, is reachable for 2^k, and only [p] is unreachable for odd p. The converse directions follow from the one-line odd-divisor invariant. So both A292728 conjectures were essentially settled in the companion entry, and the PR mostly formalises known facts. Caveat: Neder's formulas carry no written proof in the entry, so this 'known' rests on an OEIS formula claim rather than a published paper.

But the PR body itself says it follows the nil-ring counterexample of Adamczewski, Bohmler and Marczinzik, 'A counterexample to Kothe's conjecture and a question of Rowen' (arXiv:2609.07996, submitted 7 Sep 2026). The merged file is a disproof, a 30-dimensional counterexample. Its own header calls it a port of Maxence Faldor's Lean disproof following Lai, Lim and Ren, 'Pierce-Birkhoff conjecture is false' (arXiv:2609.10420, 9 Sep 2026, Theorem 7). So the conjecture was already refuted in the literature (Wikipedia still lists it as open). This is a formalization of a known result.

So it is a genuine refutation, but already published two-plus months before this PR (27 Nov 2026).

The proof gives F(N) <= sqrt(N) + 0.9434 N^{1/4} for all N >= 10^24, by a new 13-kernel certificate for Hou–Zhao's smoothing method. That is valid but improves 0.94349 only to 0.9434. A stronger bound was already published: Carter, O'Bryant and Tao, 'On the diameter and distribution of Sidon sets' (arXiv:2610.36207, 26 Oct 2026), Corollary 1.2, give |A| <= N^{1/2} + 0.94304 N^{1/4} + 0.44466 for Sidon A ⊆ [1,N] with |A| >= 483. Together with the trivial case |A| < 483, this already satisfies the formal statement with c = 0.94304. The upstream reference to HZ26 as the record is out of date, so the improvement asked for was already known.

Green35.green_35.lower.note: The formal 'lower' statement only asks for a valid lower bound for c(p) that beats sqrt(4/7) ≈ 0.75593 at p = 2 (or 0.64 at p = ∞). That is a variant of Green's 'estimate c_p'. The proof gives c(2) >= 473/625 = 0.7568 by a polynomial-kernel Fourier argument, and sets the answer to 0 at every p ≠ 2. A better bound was in the literature long before. E. P. White, 'An almost-tight L^2 autoconvolution inequality' (arXiv:2210.16437, 2022), Theorem 1, proves 0.574635728 <= inf ||f*f||_2^2 for real-valued f on a unit interval with ∫f = 1, i.e. c(2) >= 0.75805; restricting to nonnegative f only raises the infimum. White also cites Martin–O'Bryant's earlier 0.574575 (c(2) >= 0.75801). Both exceed 0.7568, so 'improving sqrt(4/7)' was already done (the upstream docstring is out of date), and this bound is weaker than the known one.

Erdos878.erdos_878.parts.v.note: The statement H ~ answer is an answer-style question, and the proof supplies the explicit equivalent H(x) ~ x * sum_{p <= (log x)^2} e^{-r_p(x)}/p * (r_p(x) + log p/(p-1)), where r_p(x) = log x - floor(log_p x) log p, proved with a Selberg-sieve tail bound. As an asymptotic formula this is a substantive, non-tautological answer to Erdős's 'find an asymptotic formula for H(x)'. However, the file's own header says it is a single-file port of rivkalipko/erdos-878-asymptotics (Rivka Lipkovitz with OpenAI Codex, PALOMAR-2026-11-19), a public Lean proof of exactly this formula that predates the 2026-11-27 merge. erdosproblems.com/878 has not been updated (0 proof claims, and no forum comment on part (v)). So this re-formalises an already-public result rather than giving a new one.

Erdos1032.erdos_1032.note: The formal statement is faithful: there exist c>0 and infinitely many n with a 4-critical graph (vertex- and edge-critical, chromatic number 4) on Fin n of minimum degree >= cn. The extra vertex-criticality is harmless because positive minimum degree excludes isolated vertices. The disproof shows every such graph has minimum degree o(n), using a bounded-depth list-colouring branching plus 2-SAT certificates whose union has linearly many edges, and edge-criticality then forces all edges into the union. The file's header says it formalises EthanYang's sparse-obstruction argument. That disproof was Lean-verified and approved on conjectures.io (verified 24 Oct 2026, certified 28 Oct 2026), before this 2026-11-27 merge. erdosproblems.com/1032 still lists the problem as open with 0 proof claims, but the result was already public, so this is a re-formalisation.

Koethe.KotherConjecture.variants.le_Koth.note: The statement (every nil left ideal lies in the Köthe radical, the sum of all nil two-sided ideals) is a standard equivalent of Köthe's conjecture and is formalised faithfully (Ideal R = left ideal; IsNil = all elements nilpotent). The disproof builds a ring (a unital subring of a banded incidence algebra over the algebraic closure of Q, generated by three weighted shifts) with a nil two-sided ideal I such that a 2x2 companion-square matrix over I is not nilpotent. This is Krempa's matrix form, and the proof passes to the le_KotherRadical form through the upstream column-ideal lemmas. It contains no sorry or axioms. But Köthe's conjecture was already refuted in September 2026: Adamczewski-Böhmler-Marczinzik, arXiv:2609.07996 (7 Sep 2026), plus the GPT-6 Astra Lean disproof of the same Krempa matrix form (tadamcz/koethe), which uses a very similar shift-operator/pencil/common-zero construction. So this is a formalisation of a known result.

OeisA114216.conjecture.note: The formal statement 'a(n) != 1 for all n > 33900' is a faithful reading of OEIS A114216's question 'Is a(33900) the last term equal to 1?', and the recurrence matches OEIS (a(n) is the odd part of a(n-1)+prime(n)). The disproof kernel-checks a(78493252) = 1 (567791839 + 1579691809 = 2^31) using a wheel sieve with decide +kernel and no native_decide. That counterexample was already found by Donovan Johnson in May 2010 and is recorded in OEIS A114217 (term 78493252) and A114218 (k=31), as the proof header itself says. The A114216 comment is simply stale, so this formalises a known result.

Green31.green_31.variants.upper_eventual.note: The statement asks for a bound F(N) <= answer(N) for all large N, with answer(N) - sqrt N <= c N^{1/4} + C for some c < 0.94349 (the Hou-Zhao constant). This faithfully encodes 'improve the [HZ26] upper bound', but that is a moving record, not Green's original threshold. The proof gives c = 0.9434 via an explicit 13-component certificate (sqrt(ab) ≈ 0.94335) inside Hou-Zhao's vector-valued smoothing framework, and appears sound (decide +kernel, no native_decide). However, smaller constants in the same framework were posted publicly before the 2026-11-27 merge, on the erdosproblems.com #30 forum: 0.94325 (JoshMadeiros, 17 Aug 2026, with Lean-checked covering inequalities) and 0.9428096 (johnakwei, 5 Oct 2026, which also argues 2*sqrt(2)/3 is the method's limit). Both are unrefereed, but they already beat 0.94349 by more than this proof does. This is a weaker re-derivation of an already-achieved improvement.

Erdos36.erdos_36.variants.upper.note: The formal statement asks for limsup M(N)/N <= c with c < 0.380926853433087, which is Haugland's old bound. erdosproblems.com/36 records that this was already beaten: the current record is c < 0.380876 (TTT-Discover, 2026), improving on AlphaEvolve [GGTW25] and Haugland. The proof establishes limsup <= 0.3809, using a 512-bin step function block-averaged from the atrislabs/records construction plus a probabilistic rounding argument. That is valid but weaker than the published record. The catalogue threshold is stale, so this proves an already-known (indeed already-improved) bound.

Erdos1063.erdos_1063.better_upper.note: The statement asks for an answer g with n_k = O(g) and g = o(k * lcm(1..k-1)), improving Cambie's bound; this is a reasonable reading of 'estimate n_k'. The proof gives g(k) = exp(k/log k * (log log k + log log log k + log 2)). The upstream formal-conjectures file itself records exactly this bound as research solved (erdos_1063.variants.subexponential_upper_bound), formally proved by the LEAP agent (lfsong-google fork, commit ff33e501). The OMA file's header says it is adapted from that proof, and it uses the same folded-pigeonhole/Chebyshev construction (n_le_folded_pigeonhole_product appears verbatim in the source). So this is a port of a known formal result.

Erdos357.erdos_357.parts.ii.bigO_version.note: This is an answer-style variant: find g with g = O(f), where f(n) is the largest increasing sequence in [1,n] with distinct consecutive-block sums. The proof takes g = sqrt n. That is exactly the order of Weisenberg's known lower bound f(n) >= (2+o(1)) sqrt n, cited on erdosproblems.com/357 and recorded upstream as solved (erdos_357.variants.weisenberg). The file declares itself a 'PORT OF A PUBLIC PROOF, not a new result' (KitaKen1/erdos-357-sqrt-lower-bound). The upstream note itself warns that such answer variants admit easy solutions, and this one adds nothing on how f grows (whether f(n) = o(n) is still open).

Green77.green_77.note: The statement 'exists o -> 0 with alpha(n) << n^{-2+o(n)}', where alpha(n) is the Heilbronn sup-min triangle area in the unit disc (Erdos507.alpha), faithfully encodes Green's question of whether there is always a triangle of area at most n^{-2+o(1)}. The disproof gives arbitrarily large n-point sets with every triangle of area >= n^{-2+eta} for a fixed eta > 0, then translates them into the disc. The file states it is a port of OpenAI's openai/math Lean development (OAI.Problem355.heilbronn_power_lower_bound, family 191, 'A power improvement in the Heilbronn triangle lower bound'), whose preprint is dated September 2026. So the power-saving lower bound refuting Green 77 was already public before this 2026-11-27 merge.

Erdos357.erdos_357.parts.ii.littleO_vers.note: This is an answer-style variant: find g with g = o(f). The proof takes g = sqrt n / log n and combines the known sqrt n = O(f) (Weisenberg's f(n) >= (2+o(1)) sqrt n, on erdosproblems.com/357 and solved upstream) with the trivial sqrt n / log n = o(sqrt n). The file declares itself a port of a public proof (KitaKen1/erdos-357-sqrt-lower-bound). It is strictly weaker than the bigO variant and gives no new information about the growth of f, so it is a formalisation of a known result.

Erdos143.erdos_143.parts.ii.note: The statement says every well-separated A in (1, inf) (|kx - y| >= 1 for distinct x, y and k >= 1) has sum 1/(x log x) < inf, which is faithful to Erdős's first question. The proof disproves it with an explicit countable set of rationals in [2, inf) whose weight diverges, and checks that the set meets all the WellSeparatedSet hypotheses. The file states it is a port of Mattia Apicella's Lean development (mapice/erdos-143-candidate-disproof, commit 0f4b969). erdosproblems.com/143 already links that commit as 'a formalised negative answer to the first question', and the catalogue's erdosState is 'solved'. So this formalises a known result.

Erdos14.erdos_14.parts.ii.note: The statement 'there exists A with |[1,N] \ B| = o(sqrt N)', where B is the set of integers with exactly one representation as a sum of two elements of A, faithfully encodes Erdős's second question. The proof shows that every A has at least sqrt(N)/12000 non-uniquely represented integers for large N. The file says the argument and helper lemmas are adapted from L. Kruer and J. Kohlmeyer (liamkruer.com, Erdos14_PartII_Counterexample.lean). erdosproblems.com/14 already states that the answer to the second question is no (|[1,N] \ B| >> N^{1/2}) and links a formalised proof, and the catalogue's erdosState is 'solved'. So this is a known result.

MeanValueProblem.mean_value_problem.note: The statement is Smale's mean value conjecture with K = 1 (the K argument is unused). It says that for deg p >= 2 and any z there is a critical point c with |p(z)-p(c)|/|z-c| <= |p'(z)|, which is faithful; Lean's x/0 = 0 convention only makes the claim easier. The proof refutes it with a large-degree polynomial approximating a model built on the cubic lemniscate |(z^3+36i)/sqrt 1297| <= 1. But the K = 1 conjecture was already disproved in September 2026: a GPT-6 Astra Lean disproof against the same formal-conjectures statement (tadamcz/mean-value-problem, a quartic four-petal version of the same normal-re-entry idea), explained in Adamczewski-Colbrook, arXiv:2610.36158 (26 Oct 2026), which gives an explicit degree-29,984 example. This proof uses a different lemniscate but proves a known result.

Koethe.KotherConjecture.variants.matrixO.note: The statement Nil*(M_n(R)) = M_n(Nil*(R)) for every finite index type n is a standard equivalent (Krempa) of Köthe's conjecture and is formalised faithfully. The proof file is identical to the le_KotherRadical disproof except for the final bridge: it reuses the same ring with a nil ideal I and a non-nilpotent W in M_2(I), and deduces a contradiction via isNil_kotheRadical and the ULift(Fin 2) reindexing. Köthe's conjecture, in exactly this matrix form, was already refuted in September 2026: Adamczewski-Böhmler-Marczinzik, arXiv:2609.07996, and the GPT-6 Astra Lean disproof of KotherConjecture.variants.general_matrix (tadamcz/koethe). So this is a formalisation of a known result.

Erdos161.erdos_161.parts.ii.note: The statement says that for t >= 3 and all alpha, beta in (0, 1/2), F^{(t)}(n, alpha) = Theta(F^{(t)}(n, beta)), using balancedColoringThreshold. This faithfully encodes 'for fixed t >= 3, do all positive densities below 1/2 give the same asymptotic order?' (the 'one jump at 0' guess). The proof file itself says the result is Corollary 3 of Dhruv Mubayi, 'Large blow-ups of uniform hypergraphs', arXiv:2611.33108 (posted 24 Nov 2026), and it formalises Mubayi's blow-up theorem. Mubayi's abstract gives the order (log n)^{1/(k-1)} for every fixed 0 < alpha < 1/2 and refers to Erdős's $500 question. The t=3 case was already Conlon-Fox-Sudakov 2011. The published solution predates the 2026-11-27 merge, so this is a formalisation of a known result (the erdosproblems page is not yet updated).

WrittenOnTheWallII.GraphConjecture72.con.reason: The disproof is correct for the reading ceil(ecc_avg + maxL/3) <= tree(G), which the formal-conjectures reviewer confirmed against the source, but it is not new. RhudeJJJJ/Gebendorfer published a Lean-certified 31-vertex counterexample to exactly this reading in formal-conjectures PR #7666 / issue #7662 on 28 Oct 2026, and the reviewer approved it. VibeMathed records that 'the stronger reading that divides only L by three is false', going back to a 23 Jul 2026 post. A separate 19-vertex Palomar entry (PALOMAR-2026-11-26-000022) was also first published on 26 Nov 2026 at 04:44 UTC, before PR #620 was opened (26 Nov, 23:24 UTC). It should be listed as known, not as an open problem solved.
